'''Suzanne "Big Suze"<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bullandbearmcgill.com/meme-ing-mcgill|work=The Bull and Bear|title=Meme-ing McGill|date=7 February 2018|access-date=5 January 2026}}</ref> Fortier''' {{post-nominals|country=CAN|OC|FRSC}} (born November 11, 1949)<ref name="GlobeBio">{{cite news|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/report-on-business/careers/careers-leadership/mcgill-principal-and-vice-chancellor-completes-full-circle/article20708312/?page=all|work=The Globe and Mail|title=McGill principal and vice-chancellor completes full circle|date=19 September 2014 |access-date=September 30, 2014}}</ref> is a Canadian crystallographer who was the 17th [[List of McGill University people#List of principals|Principal]] and Vice-Chancellor of [[McGill University]].

==Early life and education==

Fortier was born in [[Saint-Timothée, Quebec]], a town on Île-de-Salaberry in the [[St. Lawrence River]]. Her parents ran a small local hotel. She grew up speaking only French and attended a small local convent, which served as elementary school.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thefreelibrary.com/Ardent+administrator:+how+Suzanne+Fortier's+unmistakable+enthusiasm+...-a0274790314|title=Ardent administrator: how Suzanne Fortier's unmistakable enthusiasm for Canadian science began with a passion for solving the "beautiful puzzles" of the structure of matter. - Free Online Library|website=www.thefreelibrary.com|access-date=2017-10-26}}</ref> A nun who taught chemistry and was enthusiastic about the subject inspired her to pursue science.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hoag|first=Hannah|date=8 March 2006|title=Suzanne Fortier, president, Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=440|issue=7081|pages=252|doi=10.1038/nj7081-252a|s2cid=155850217|issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free}}</ref>

She was among the first group of girls admitted to the local [[CEGEP]], where she and a friend decided to enter the 1968 Quebec provincial science fair.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Calamai|first=Peter|date=May 2011|title=Ardent administrator: how Suzanne Fortier's unmistakable enthusiasm for Canadian science began with a passion for solving the "beautiful puzzles" of the structure of matter|journal=Canadian Chemical News|volume=63|issue=5}}</ref> Their project on the diffraction of sound waves interested a [[crystallography|crystallographer]] from McGill University who was attending the science fair, and who invited Fortier and her friend to visit his lab. This visit further confirmed her interest in science generally and crystallography in particular, a field of study that she has said "present[s] you with beautiful puzzles to solve. There are incredible pictures that you get of the structure of matter."<ref name=":0" />

Fortier entered McGill University, receiving a Bachelor of Science degree in 1972. She won an NRC Canada Post Graduate Scholarship and entered directly into a PhD program in crystallography. Her supervisor was [[Gabrielle Donnay]].

During her PhD work, she attended a talk by U.S. mathematician Herbert Hauptman, who would later win the 1985 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and who studied directed methods for determining crystal structures. After being awarded her PhD in 1976, Fortier worked on biophysics for six years at the Medical Foundation of Buffalo, Inc., a private institute where Hauptman was research director (now the Hauptman-Woodward Medical Research Institute).

==Academic career==

In 1982, she joined the Department of Chemistry of [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] in [[Kingston, Ontario]] as an assistant professor. She was the first woman to be hired by the department.{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} She was interested in using [[artificial intelligence]] and other mathematical and machine learning techniques to determine the structure of proteins. In 1993, she was cross-appointed to the Department of Computer Science. She later served as Queen's Vice-Principal for Research from 1995 to 2000, and then as Vice-Principal for Academics from 2000 to 2005.{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}}

She took a leave from Queen's to become the President of the [[Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council]] (NSERC), a [[Canadian government]] agency that provides grants for research in the [[natural sciences]] and in [[engineering]]. She served as head of NSERC from January 16, 2006<ref name="NSERC-in">{{Cite web|url=http://www.nserc-crsng.gc.ca/NSERC-CRSNG/President-Presidente/Biography-Biographie_eng.asp|title=Biography: Dr. Suzanne Fortier (Wayback machine cache)|date=2009-06-10|publisher=Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130107230804/http://www.nserc-crsng.gc.ca/NSERC-CRSNG/President-Presidente/Biography-Biographie_eng.asp|archive-date=January 7, 2013|url-status=unfit|access-date=21 August 2010}}
</ref> until March 4, 2013.<ref name="NSERC-out">{{Cite web|url=http://www.nserc-crsng.gc.ca/NSERC-CRSNG/ProgramNewsDetails-NouvellesDesProgrammesDetails_eng.asp?ID=395|title=Statement from Dr. Suzanne Fortier|last=Suzanne|first=Fortier|date=2013-03-05|publisher=Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada|access-date=3 September 2013}}
</ref>

In September 2013, Fortier was appointed the principal and vice-chancellor of McGill University.

Fortier's current salary at McGill is $390,000 with a discretionary bonus of up to twenty percent. Her contract was made public in 2013 by the university.

She was a member of the Advisory Council on Economic Growth, which advised the Canadian Finance Minister [[Bill Morneau]] on economic policies to achieve long-term [[sustainable growth]]. The Council called for a gradual increase in permanent [[immigration to Canada]] to 450,000 people a year.<ref>{{cite news |title=Fortier, Ragan part of Advisory Council on Economic Growth |url=https://reporter.mcgill.ca/fortier-ragan-part-of-federal-advisory-council-on-economic-growth/ |work=McGill Reporter |date=May 17, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Influential Liberal advisers want Canadian population to triple by 2100 |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/3020783/influential-liberal-advisers-want-canadian-population-to-triple-by-2100/ |work=[[Global News]] |date=October 23, 2016}}</ref>

In 2022, Fortier announced her retirement from the role of principal and vice-chancellor of McGill University effective August 31, 2022.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Friesen|first=Joe|date=2022-01-07|title=McGill University principal Suzanne Fortier to step down in August|language=en-CA|work=The Globe and Mail|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-mcgill-university-principal-suzanne-fortier-to-step-down-in-august/|access-date=2022-01-08}}</ref>

==Honours==
Fortier was awarded a total of three honorary doctorates from [[Thompson Rivers University]], [[Carleton University]], and the [[University of Glasgow]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mcgill.ca/principal/about/biography|title=Office of the Principal and Vice-Chancellor: Biography|website=McGill University|access-date=2019-01-21}}</ref> In 1997, she received the [[Clara Benson|Clara Benson Award]] for distinguished contributions to chemistry by a woman. Fortier was also honored with the [[Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal]] in 2012.
